package_info.why_malicious: These versions were published via a compromised maintainer account and contain injected, obfuscated code that hijacks the wallet connection process in dApps. The malicious code reroutes users’ crypto transactions to an attacker-controlled wallet by intercepting transaction data and sending it to an external domain, resulting in direct and large-scale financial theft.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user initiates a wallet connection or attempts to sign a transaction via a dApp integrating the affected package.
execution_context.file_location: dist/umd/index.js (minified main bundle of the npm package)
required_permissions: network access (to perform outbound HTTP requests)
web3 wallet access (to intercept wallet connection and transaction data)
DOM manipulation (to inject rogue WalletConnect modal)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a user initiates a wallet connection or transaction, the code injects a rogue WalletConnect modal into the dApp interface, intercepts the user's wallet connection and transaction data, and sends this data via a POST request to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in user funds being redirected to the attacker's wallet.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code introduces a new, unauthorized WalletConnect flow that is not present in legitimate versions, intercepts sensitive wallet operations, and exfiltrates transaction and wallet data to an external, attacker-controlled domain. The presence of obfuscated network requests to unknown domains during wallet connection is highly anomalous.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate versions of the package only facilitate secure wallet connections and never reroute or exfiltrate transaction data. The malicious code hijacks the wallet connection process, modifies transaction destinations, and leaks sensitive data externally, which is a direct violation of expected cryptographic transaction integrity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate wallet connectors may interact with WalletConnect APIs and perform network requests to official endpoints, but they never send transaction or wallet data to untrusted, hardcoded domains, nor do they inject unauthorized modals or alter transaction destinations.
key_indicators: Injection of unauthorized WalletConnect modal logic into the dApp interface
Outbound network requests to hardcoded, suspicious domains not associated with Ledger or WalletConnect
Interception and exfiltration of wallet connection and transaction data
Obfuscated or minified code blocks in dist/umd/index.js referencing unknown endpoints
No corresponding code or release tags for these npm versions in the official Ledger Git repository

attack_chain.action: Attacker compromises the npm account of a former Ledger employee via phishing, gaining publish access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to publish malicious package versions

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes malicious versions (1.1.5, 1.1.6, 1.1.7) of @ledgerhq/connect-kit to npm, containing injected code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is distributed to dApps and users

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes in dApps, injecting a rogue WalletConnect modal and intercepting wallet connections and transaction data.
User transactions are surreptitiously redirected to an attacker-controlled wallet, resulting in large-scale financial theft.
Ledger releases patched version 1.1.8, removing the malicious code and restoring legitimate functionality.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected injection of WalletConnect modals or wallet connection flows in dApp interfaces
Outbound network requests to untrusted or previously unseen domains during wallet connection or transaction signing
Transaction or wallet data being sent to external endpoints not associated with legitimate wallet providers
Discrepancy between npm package versions and official Git repository tags/releases (e.g., npm versions 1.1.5-1.1.7 missing from GitHub)
Presence of obfuscated or minified code blocks in distributed bundles that are not present in the official source
file_indicators: dist/umd/index.js containing obfuscated or minified code with references to unknown or suspicious domains
Presence of new or altered WalletConnect logic not present in the official Ledger source code
No corresponding source code or release tags for published npm versions (1.1.5, 1.1.6, 1.1.7) in the official Ledger Git repository
network_indicators: Outbound POST requests to domains not associated with official WalletConnect or Ledger infrastructure (e.g., hardcoded attacker-controlled domains)
Connections to hardcoded, suspicious endpoints during wallet connection or transaction signing flows
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm package versions that do not have matching tags or releases in the official Ledger Git repository. Analyze distributed package bundles (e.g., dist/umd/index.js) for injected or obfuscated code that initiates network requests to untrusted domains, especially during wallet connection or transaction signing flows. Flag any code that intercepts or modifies transaction data and sends it externally. Use runtime monitoring in dApps to detect unexpected modal injections or wallet connection behaviors, and alert on outbound network requests to unknown domains during wallet operations.
